speaker: AI
text: Tell me about a system you designed that had to handle a lot of traffic.

speaker: CANDIDATE
text: At my last internship I designed the checkout service for a retail app that handled about 3,000 requests per second at peak. I split it into an order service and a payment service, put a queue between them, and cached product lookups in Redis. That cut p99 latency from 800 ms to about 180 ms.

speaker: AI
text: How did you keep the order and payment services consistent?

speaker: CANDIDATE
text: I used idempotency keys on every payment request and an outbox table in the order service. A worker published outbox rows to the queue, so a crash between the database write and the publish could not lose an event. Duplicate deliveries were safe because the payment handler ignored keys it had already processed.

speaker: AI
text: Tell me about a bug that was hard to track down.

speaker: CANDIDATE
text: We saw intermittent 500s that only appeared under load. I added structured logs with a request id and traced it to a connection pool that was created per request instead of per process, so we exhausted Postgres connections. I moved the pool to a singleton and added a load test to catch a regression.

speaker: AI
text: How do you approach code review?

speaker: CANDIDATE
text: I read the diff for correctness first, then ask whether the tests would catch a regression. I keep feedback specific to the code rather than the person, and I would rather leave one clear comment than rewrite someone's work for them. If a change is too large I ask for it to be split so it is easier to reason about.
